pairs.evidence_text: The estimation results present that ICT skills, a measure incorporating an individual’s proficiency in ICT skills and their utilization in the workplace, has a positive effect on the wages of the older workers aged 50–64 with a high level of education or in a skill-intensive occupation.

In Korea, along with the rapid growth of the information and communications technology (ICT) sector and the heavy investment in new technologies in the economy (Lee, Song, & Kwak, 2020), acquisition of ICT skills has also been active—for instance, through formal education.1 Korea’s ICT use in education essentially began with improving students’ computer literacy, followed by continued reinforcement of human and physical infrastructure; based on this approach, there were increased learning opportunities using ICT.

Another notable feature is that the participation rate in on-the-job training for the older age group in Korea is lower than other OECD countries, including the United States (US), Japan, and Nordic countries (World Bank, 2016).

If older workers are more educated or continuously develop their human capital after their formal education by adapting to new technologies, having longer work experience, participating in on-the-job training, and equipping themselves with proper skills, their productivity might not necessarily be lower than that of younger workers.

In Korea, the observed wage, especially higher wage among older workers, must be determined not only by labor productivity, but also institutional features such as a seniority-based wage and promotion system and labor union. 3 We include a gender dummy in the wage equation to control for the wage differential by gender.
